notesStmt.note: As this manuscript contains a draft of the introduction to a lecture that Whitman gave in April 1890, it must date from before that time, likely only shortly before, sometime early in 1890.

This manuscript contains a passage, with corrections, that appears almost verbatim in "Walt Whitman's Last Public," included within the "Memoranda" section of Complete Prose Works, published in 1892. In the piece, written in third person, Whitman describes the speech he gave on the 25th anniversary of Abraham Lincoln's death at the Art Rooms, in Philadelphia, on April 15, 1890. The passage appearing in this manuscript is ostensibly the verbatim opening address of the talk, although as we do not have a written version of the talk, it is impossible to be certain. Whitman seems to have borrowed some phrases in this manuscript from the printed version of the lecture "Death of Abraham Lincoln," delivered in New York in 1879, in Philadelphia in 1880 and in Boston in 1881, portions of which were published in various venues before finally appearing in Complete Prose Works.

body.p: Of Abraham Lincoln, ‸bearing testimony, twenty five years after his death—and of that death—I am no my friends for a few minutes before you,. bearing testimony Few realize of the great days, the great, ‸historic and esthetic personalities we have justlately pass'd through. Abraham Lincoln, ‸familiar, our own, an Illinoisian, ‸modern yet tallying of ‸ancient Moses, Joshua, ‸Ulysses, Socrates, Rabelais, or later ‸Michel Angelo, Cromwell, and grander in some respects than any of them; Abraham Lincoln that makes ‸such as Homer, Plutarch, Shakspere, possible. My subject to you my friends this evening for my 40 or 50 minutes' talk is the Death of Abraham Lincoln,this man, and how that death will affect America.
